scenario: AITA for causing a friend to drop out of school? | I know my title sounds bad. I (17F) am currently in my senior year of school. Friend1 (18F) recently lost her dad to an accidental overdose. Her dad died the morning of a party our whole friend group was meant to attend. Friend2(17F) had no alcohol for this party (I know we're underage but in our country it's 18 not 21). Upon hearing about Friend1's dad on our groupchat, she said nothing. Fine. Whatever. That's none of my business. A shit thing to do considering they're close but not my place, I was more preoccupied with trying to make sure Friend1 was ok so I didn't want to bring it up. Our friend then messaged on this chat asking Friend1 if she was still going to the party and if not could she give her any alcohol she had bought for it. I thought this was absolutely out of order and I messaged her privately and send quite strong messages. I said it was a really cunty thing to do ON the day her dad died. I called her pathetic and said she should be ashamed of herself. This happened last weekend. She left our groupchat. Went to the party and then came to school on Monday and dropped out. She had said repeatedly before that she was only in school this year to hang out with us. Friend1 is obviously currently preoccupied with famy stuff and not petty friend drama but she did tell Friend2 to fuck off as well. I spoke to her briefly about it before I messaged privately. I'm now being blamed by friends of Friend2 who were not in the groupchat for her leaving school. They are saying I helped bully her out of school. AITA? I'm beginning to think I was because of how strongly worded my message was.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing or not in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened step by step. First, my friend Friend1 lost her dad to an accidental overdose. That's really sad and unexpected, especially since it happened on the morning of a party that our whole friend group was supposed to attend. I can imagine how shocked everyone must have been. Friend2, who is 17, didn't have any alcohol for the party. I know that in our country, the legal drinking age is 18, so she's underage. But that's not the main issue here. The problem started when Friend2 messaged the group chat after hearing about Friend1's dad. She asked Friend1 if she was still going to the party and if not, could she give her any alcohol she had bought. That seemed really insensitive to me because Friend1 was dealing with a huge loss. I thought Friend2's message was out of order, so I messaged her privately. I was pretty strong in my words, calling her actions "cunty" and saying she was pathetic and should be ashamed. That was last weekend. After that, Friend2 left the group chat, went to the party, and then came to school on Monday and dropped out. She had mentioned before that she was only in school this year to hang out with us, so her dropping out seems significant. Friend1 is obviously dealing with family stuff and isn't focused on petty drama, but she did tell Friend2 to fuck off as well. I had talked to Friend1 briefly about it before I sent my private message, so I think I was trying to support her. Now, I'm being blamed by Friend2's friends, who weren't in the group chat, for bullying her out of school. They're saying I helped bully her. I'm starting to think maybe I was too harsh with my words, and that's why Friend2 left school. So, the question is: Did I do the right thing by confronting Friend2 so strongly, or was it wrong because it led to Friend2 dropping out of school? I need to consider a few things here. First, was Friend2's message really that bad? She asked Friend1 about the party and the alcohol. Given that Friend1's dad had just died, it's understandable that this would be hurtful. But is it the worst thing someone could do? Maybe, but I think it's important to consider the context. Second, how did I respond? I used strong language, calling her names and shaming her. That's definitely harsh. While I was trying to stand up for Friend1, my approach might have been too aggressive. It's possible that my message made Friend2 feel attacked, leading her to leave the group and eventually drop out of school. Third, the impact on Friend2. She was already in a vulnerable position, given that she was only in school to hang out with us. If she felt isolated or unsupported, dropping out might have been her way of coping. My strong words might have contributed to her feeling alone and pushed her to make that decision. On the other hand, I was trying to support Friend1 and stand up for what I thought was right. It's important to call out insensitive behavior, but maybe there's a better way to do it without using such harsh language. I also need to consider the role of Friend2's friends. They're blaming me without being part of the conversation. That might be because they don't have the full context, but it's also possible that they're taking sides without understanding the situation fully. In the end, I think my intention was good, but my method was flawed. Using strong, hurtful words might have had unintended consequences, like pushing Friend2 away and contributing to her decision to drop out. It's a tough situation because I want to support my friends, but I also don't want to cause more harm. So, reflecting on this, I think I might have overreacted. While it's important to address insensitive behavior, doing so with kindness and understanding could have been a better approach. Maybe talking to Friend2 calmly or involving a mutual friend to mediate could have helped resolve the issue without escalating it. I also need to consider how to make things right. Maybe reaching out to Friend2 to apologize for the harsh words and express my concern for her well-being could help mend the relationship. It's important to communicate in a way that shows I care about her feelings too, even though I was upset at the time. In summary, while I thought I was doing the right thing by confronting Friend2, the way I did it might have been wrong because it led to negative consequences for her. It's a lesson in how the method of addressing issues can be as important as the intent behind them.
